doc.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Family, identity and the Two Flowers metaphor
title: Growing up Chinese-American in the suburbs: language, assimilation and taboo China
summary: His parents' Cantonese, suburban assimilation versus Chinatown, and China as a taboo subject until the early seventies.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Were your parents interested in integrating themselves as much into American culture as they could? Or did they keep their own cultural identity intact?

Well they both spoke Cantonese, but because they were from different villages they didn’t speak together. But my mother, even though she still retains Cantonese at the third grade level, doesn’t speak to my daughter, who is in a Chinese immersion program. This was during a period, and still continues today in an English-only environment. And the assimilation process of Chinese-Americans was very distinct than say Japanese Americans in the way that Chinese-Americans or Chinese-Americans that lived in Chinatown, was based more on the immigrant experience and they spoke the language, they ate the food, there is the customs and mannerisms, the Cantonese opera, mahjong. Whereas being removed and living in a predominantly white suburb area, you became American and you spoke only English. And I had no connection with China simply because during the fifties, the McCarthy period, and the 1960s, you couldn’t even talk about China. It was taboo until 19, what was it, early seventies when Kissinger and Nixon came to visit to China. That began to loosen. I mean in the public schools I think you could learn the Japanese language, but the Chinese language was not offered. I mean there’s Chinese schools I think in San Francisco, Chinatown, you could go there. But if you’re in the white suburbs. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

Yeah. I have this memory of having a write a report on Communist China in high school and having to get information from the London Embassy, because they didn’t have anything in the States here. Interesting how things change.

Yeah there was only I think one film about China that I remember seeing when I think I was in high school. It was called “Misunderstanding China.” And I think it wasn’t shown to me yet until the early seventies.
